“I will submit to you. Your face tells me that you understand I can do nothing else. I know you are faithful.”

The old man kissed her, ushered her hastily into his room, and locked the door. Then he hurried back to the Doctor, opened the window, drew the blind partly aside, placed a hand upon the Doctor’s arm, and looked with him into the courtyard.

They looked upon a gathering of women and men, neither numerous nor closely packed enough to fill the yard: no more than forty or fifty altogether. Those occupying the house had admitted them through the gate, and they had rushed to work at the grindstone, evidently erected for their use in this convenient, secluded place.

But what dreadful workers, and what dreadful labour!

Two men frantically turned the grindstone’s double handle. As its revolutions brought their faces upward and tossed back their long hair, those faces appeared more savage and cruel than the wildest barbarians in their fiercest disguises. They wore pasted-on eyebrows and moustaches. Their monstrous countenances were covered in sweat and blood, distorted by their howling, their eyes glaring and staring with brutish excitement and sleeplessness. As the ruffians kept turning, their tangled locks swung forward over their eyes and backward across their necks. Women held wine to their lips so they could drink. With blood dripping, wine spilling, and sparks streaming from the stone, the whole malignant air about them seemed composed of gore and flame. Not a single creature in the group could be seen without a bloody smear. Men bare to the waist, stained over body and limbs, shouldered each other to reach the sharpening-stone. Men in every variety of rag carried the stain upon their rags. Others were devilishly adorned in plundered women’s ribbons, silk, and lace, each trifle dyed through and through. The hatchets, knives, swords, and bayonets brought to be sharpened were all red with it. Some notched swords were bound to their bearers’ wrists with linen strips and scraps of clothing; the fastenings varied, but all were steeped in that same colour. When the frantic owners snatched their weapons from the stream of sparks and dashed into the streets, the same red burned in their maddened eyes—eyes that any spectator not yet brutalised would have surrendered twenty years of life to turn to stone with a well-aimed gun.

“Keep in mind the points I have emphasized: the strange voice, the extraordinary agility, and the complete lack of motive for such a horrifying murder. Now consider the killing itself. A woman was strangled by hand and pushed headfirst up a chimney. Ordinary killers do not murder in this way, and certainly do not dispose of bodies like this. You must agree that forcing the corpse into the chimney was extremely strange, wholly unlike what we expect of human behavior, even from the most depraved people. Think, too, of the strength needed to push her body up that narrow opening so firmly that several people working together could barely pull it down.

“Now consider the other evidence of astonishing strength. Thick locks of gray human hair lay on the hearth—very thick locks, torn out by the roots. You know how much force it takes to pull even twenty or thirty hairs from someone’s head at once. You saw those locks just as I did. Pieces of scalp still clung to their roots, a hideous sight. This clearly showed the enormous power used to tear out perhaps half a million hairs at a time. The old woman’s throat was not simply cut: her head was completely separated from her body, using only a razor. Notice, too, the animal savagery of these acts. I will not dwell on the bruises on Madame L’Espanaye’s body. Monsieur Dumas and his worthy colleague Monsieur Etienne declared that some blunt object had caused them. On that point, they are quite correct. The blunt object was plainly the stone paving in the yard. The victim fell onto it from the window overlooking the bed. Simple as this explanation now seems, the police missed it for the same reason they missed the width of the shutters. The matter of the nails had closed their minds completely to the possibility that the windows had ever been opened.

“If, in addition, you have properly considered the room’s peculiar disorder, we can now bring all these observations together. We have astonishing agility, strength beyond human ability, animal ferocity, and slaughter without a motive. We have a form of horror so grotesque that it seems entirely foreign to human nature. Finally, we have a voice whose tones sounded unfamiliar to listeners from many countries, a voice without any clear or understandable syllables.

It is scarcely four o’clock, yet winter’s sun has already gone down. No clouds hang in the clear, freezing sky to catch its sloping rays, but a faint rosy tint colours the air itself and is reflected once more upon the snow below. My dwelling is a lonely cottage on a broad, deserted heath; no living voice comes to me. The waste stretches white before my eyes, broken only by a few dark patches where the midday sun has bared the tops of pointed hillocks. There the snow, slipping as it fell, had lain less deeply than on level ground. A handful of birds peck at the solid ice upon the pools, for the frost has endured a long while.

My mind is strangely disposed. I am alone—utterly alone in the world. Misfortune’s blight has swept across me and left me withered. I know death approaches, and I am happy, even joyful. I feel my pulse: it races. I press my wasted hand against my cheek: it burns. A frail, quick spirit remains within me, giving out its final sparks. I shall never behold another winter’s snow; I believe I shall never again experience the renewing warmth of a summer sun. With this conviction I begin to set down my sorrowful history. Perhaps a tale like mine ought to perish with me; yet an impulse I cannot explain urges me forward, and I am too feeble in body and mind to withstand even the lightest prompting. When life was vigorous in me, I believed my story held a sacred horror that forbade its telling. Now, as I prepare to die, I profane those mysterious terrors. It is like the grove of the Eumenides, into which only the dying may pass; and Oedipus approaches death.

What am I setting down? I must gather my thoughts. I cannot know whether anyone except you, my friend, will read these pages, which you will receive when I am dead. I do not write to you alone, because I wish to linger over our friendship in a manner unnecessary if you were my only reader. I shall therefore tell my history as though to strangers. Often you have asked why I live apart, why I weep, and, above all, why my silence is so unyielding and unkind. Living, I dared not answer; dying, I disclose the secret. Others may turn these pages carelessly. To you, Woodville, my gentle, loving friend, they will be precious relics of a broken-hearted girl whose gratitude to you still warms her as she dies. Your tears will wet the words recounting my sorrows; I know they will, and while life remains I thank you for your compassion.
